alignment.note: Greek uses coordinating καί + aorist participle εἰσελθοῦσα ('and having entered'); the Vulgate renders this with the enclitic conjunction Cumque + pluperfect subjunctive introisset ('and when she had entered'), while the Peshitta uses a finite perfect ܥܠܬ ('she entered') coordinated by the prefixed waw in ܘܡܚܕܐ. The participial vs. finite-verb realisation is a routine translational adjustment.
εὐθὺς / ܘܡܚܕܐ / statim — 'immediately.' The Peshitta fuses the conjunction and adverb into a single token ܘܡܚܕܐ, hence its early position.

μετὰ σπουδῆς / ܒܒܛܝܠܘܬܐ / cum festinatione — 'with haste.' Greek and Latin use a preposition + noun; Syriac employs a single prepositional abstract noun (root b-T-l, here in the diligence/haste sense), semantically equivalent.
πρὸς τὸν βασιλέα / ܠܘܬ ܡܠܟܐ / ad regem — 'to the king.'

Greek ᾐτήσατο ('she asked/requested') is matched by Vulgate petivit, but the Peshitta has no discrete verb of asking, collapsing the request into the speech introduced by ܘܐܡܪܐ ('and saying'). The Syriac thus omits the explicit petition verb, expressing the demand purely through direct speech.

Greek λέγουσα and Latin dicens are bare participles; the Peshitta expands with ܘܐܡܪܐ ܠܗ ('and saying to him'), supplying the dative indirect object ܠܗ not present in the Greek or Latin. The Vulgate adds an explicit colon (token 9) marking the onset of direct speech.
θέλω / ܨܒܝܐ ܐܢܐ / Volo — 'I desire.' Syriac uses the periphrastic participle + enclitic pronoun ܨܒܝܐ ܐܢܐ to render the first-person present, a standard Syriac construction.
ἵνα / ܕ- (prefixed on ܕܬܬܠ) / ut — purposive/complementary conjunction. The Syriac fuses the conjunction with the verb as the prefix ܕ-.
ἐξαυτῆς / ܒܗܕܐ ܫܥܬܐ / protinus — 'at once / immediately.' The Peshitta renders the Greek adverb with the fuller idiom ܒܗܕܐ ܫܥܬܐ ('in this hour'), a typical Syriac periphrasis for immediacy.
δῷς / ܕܬܬܠ / des — 'you may give' (2nd singular subjunctive/imperfect).
ἐπὶ πίνακι / ܥܠ ܦܝܢܟܐ / in disco — 'on a platter.' The Syriac ܦܝܢܟܐ is itself a loanword from the same Greek πίναξ, an instance of lexical borrowing.
τὴν κεφαλήν / ܪܫܗ / caput — 'the head.' The Peshitta uses the suffixed form ܪܫܗ ('his head'), incorporating the genitive relation pronominally rather than via article + following genitive.

Ἰωάννου τοῦ βαπτιστοῦ / ܕܝܘܚܢܢ ܡܥܡܕܢܐ / Joannis Baptistæ — 'of John the Baptist.' Greek and Vulgate place the title in apposition with an article (τοῦ); the Syriac joins ܡܥܡܕܢܐ directly to ܕܝܘܚܢܢ without a repeated genitive marker.
